statement: Closing the eyes raises alpha power several-fold. In 50 screened-healthy young adults (2 min per condition, 16 sites) the global mean alpha power was 20.0 units with the eyes closed against 5.08 with them open, about four times, and alpha was higher with the eyes closed at every region, while theta was slightly higher with the eyes open; in 28 students, across-scalp mean absolute delta, theta, alpha and beta were all lower with the eyes open than closed, with frontal beta higher eyes open; in 608 adults (3,229 recordings) occipital alpha relative power was lower with the eyes open than closed (model coefficient −0.22); in 40 healthy older adults (mean age 73) relative occipital alpha power was 49.1 with the eyes closed against 18.9 open, about 2.6 times. The model multiplies the power of its three alpha regions by 4 and its beta region by 0.8 with the eyes closed, and leaves the mu rhythm unchanged (claim rhythm-mu).
note_on_site: The 50-adult study prints its powers in “kµV²” without explaining the unit; only the ratio is used, as unit-free. The 28-student study is read from its abstract (directions only). The factor 4 is the young-adult value; older adults show less.
sources: Kan DPX, Croarkin PE, Phang CK, Lee PF (2017). EEG Differences Between Eyes-Closed and Eyes-Open Conditions at the Resting Stage for Euthymic Participants. Neurophysiology 49(6):432–440. doi:10.1007/s11062-018-9706-6

statement: Higher mental workload raises frontal theta and beta and lowers alpha. A 2022 meta-analysis of 24 studies (723 participants) gave Hedges’ g = 0.68 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.95) for theta, 0.50 (0.21 to 0.79) for beta and −0.25 (−0.45 to 0.04) for alpha between lower and higher workload; in 20 adults doing an n-back task, frontal theta synchronization relative to a pre-stimulus reference rose from 8.75% at low to 18.48% at medium load and parietal alpha desynchronization from −5.63% to −24.44%, with no further change at high load; in the classic 8-subject high-density study a frontal midline theta rhythm increased and a parietocentral alpha signal decreased with memory load; spectral power features told the highest from the lowest n-back level at 80 to 90% after 2 min of data, and above chance after 2.5 s for 32 of 35 participants.

statement: “Attention”, “focus” and “engagement” metrics are ratios of fast to slow band power. The engagement index beta/(alpha + theta) was chosen in 1995 because it reflected task engagement best in a closed-loop automation experiment; a 2023 review of 82 documents catalogued 37 such ratio indexes, the most used being beta/alpha, beta/(alpha + theta), beta/theta and theta/alpha. The theta/beta ratio as an attention marker rests on group differences: a meta-analysis of 9 studies (1,253 children and adolescents with ADHD, 517 without) found effect sizes of 0.75 at ages 6 to 13 and 0.62 at 6 to 18 that shrank over the years as the ratio rose in the groups without ADHD, and judged the ratio not a reliable diagnostic measure. During cognitive tasks alpha power falls relative to pre-task eyes-open rest, more over parieto-occipital than fronto-central sites, and about 0.15 of the baseline more during mental arithmetic than during number reading (41 participants).

statement: Drowsiness and mental fatigue raise slow activity. A 2020 meta-analysis of 21 studies of mental fatigue found overall EEG power rising with a medium effect (g = 0.68), theta (g = 1.03, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.60) and alpha (g = 0.85, 0.47 to 1.43) with large effects, delta and beta with small to moderate changes, the changes largest over central sites and the theta increase above g = 1 at frontal, central and posterior sites alike; in 35 drivers in a simulator, delta and theta activity increased significantly with fatigue, and in 40 drivers the band magnitudes averaged over 19 channels rose from the alert baseline by up to 21 µV (delta), 3 µV (theta), 1.4 µV (alpha) and 1.2 µV (beta); over a monotonous drive in 52 people, slow-to-fast ratios such as (theta + alpha)/beta rose, mainly through a fall in beta; and before sleep onset the alpha rhythm spreads from the back of the head toward the front.
